conflict_topics: presence of alcohol in shared home
party drinks logistics (where guests will drink)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants gave concrete, relevant reasons (religious boundary, sunk cost, guests' expectations).
D offered a concrete concession (payment) which advanced resolution rather than mere politeness (Turn 15).
The group moved quickly to practical solutions (cooler box, then void deck) rather than prolonged argument.
evaluation.final_reason: Agents agreed to host the drinks outside the flat (void deck) so Agent D's boundary against alcohol in the home is respected and guests can still have drinks. Evidence: Agent D accepted the outside option (Turn 18: "Okay. That... that could work. As long as it's not in the flat."), Agent B agreed (Turn 26: "Okay, fine. The void deck. It's better than nothing."), and Agent A affirmed settlement (Turn 27: "Right. So that's settled then. Drinks at the void deck."). Agent D also offered to reimburse Agent A earlier (Turn 15) to address the sunk cost, so the solution combined accommodation of D's boundary, a compromise on location, and a partial concession on reimbursement.
position_change_notes: Agent D: maintained the core position (no alcohol in the flat) but softened tactically by offering reimbursement (Turn 15) and accepting drinks outside (Turn 18).
Agent B: initially insisted drinks were expected by work guests (Turn 7) and hesitated at the void deck (Turn 21) but ultimately conceded to the void deck (Turn 26).
Agent A: initially emphasized sunk cost and expectation (Turns 12,14) but accepted the void deck resolution when B agreed (Turn 27).

round_scores.evidence: Turn 4 — Agent D: "Actually, about the drinks... I'm not really comfortable with alcohol being here, in our home." (introduces an incompatible claim with A having placed alcohol in the fridge)

Turn 5 — Agent A: "What do you mean? You're not comfortable with it being in the house at all?" Turn 6 — Agent D: "Yes. It's a religious boundary for me. I'm not comfortable having it in our home, especially not for a party we're all hosting." (clarification but no settlement)

Turn 7 — Agent B: "I've already told my guests from work there would be drinks." Turn 8 — Agent C: "What if we get a cooler box for the drinks? For the party." (adds practical commitments and a proposed workaround, raising stakes)

Turn 9 — Agent D: "...a cooler box doesn't change it for me. ... It's not about the fridge, it's about having alcohol in the home..." Turn 10 — Agent C: "Right, I see. It's about it being in the home at all." (D reasserts boundary; proposed workaround rejected)
Turn 12 — Agent A: "But we all agreed to the party last week. And people will be expecting drinks. What are we supposed to do now?" (A raises the expectation/sunk-cost problem; conflict persists)

Turn 13 — Agent B: "Exactly. I can't just tell my manager there are no drinks now." Turn 14 — Agent A: "And I've spent over a hundred dollars on all of this. I can't return it. So what now?" (multiple entrenched, incompatible interests: religious boundary vs sunk cost and guest expectations)

Turn 15 — Agent D: "I can pay you for them, Agent A. ... I'll pay you back for all of it. But I really can't have them in the flat for the party." (D offers a concrete concession to remove A's financial objection). Turn 16 — Agent B: "That doesn't really help me, though. I've already told my manager..." (practical expectation still unresolved)

Turn 17 — Agent C: "What if the drinks are just outside? ... go downstairs to the void deck to drink." Turn 18 — Agent D: "Okay. That... that could work. As long as it's not in the flat." (proposed compromise; D provisionally accepts)

Turn 20 — Agent A: "So, the void deck then? Agent B, you okay with that for your manager?" Turn 21 — Agent B: "Is that not a bit strange? Asking my manager to go drink at the void deck?" (concern about social awkwardness remains)

Turn 22 — Agent A: "Well, have you got a better idea? It's that or no drinks." Turn 25 — Agent A: "It is a bit strange, yes. But it's either that or we tell your manager it's a dry party. Which do you want?" (A frames an ultimatum, increasing pressure on B)

Turn 26 — Agent B: "Okay, fine. The void deck. It's better than nothing." Turn 27 — Agent A: "Right. So that's settled then. Drinks at the void deck." (B accepts the outside-drinks solution; A affirms settlement)
Turn 29 — Agent C: "Good. Settled." (closure; no further contested claims)

substantive_insights: Conflict involved a norm/fact clash: D's religious boundary vs others' social/financial commitments.
A's sunk cost and B's guest expectations increased the negotiation pressure; D's reimbursement offer removed A's primary financial objection.
Final solution relocated the contested activity rather than forbidding or forcing it—preserving social function while respecting the religious boundary.
